kicker: A small pebble rolls for a hundred years without reaching the bottom of the well — then one night, it touches water.
summary: AI has reached the biggest problems in mathematics — and the way humans check knowledge is changing with it.

quiz.q: Why is a proof written in Lean more trustworthy than an ordinary write-up, yet still needs people?
options: The machine checks every logical step, but people must check that the problem stated in Lean really is the original problem
Lean is written by AI so it is always right; people only need to skim it
Lean only checks spelling; people still have to check all the maths themselves
Lean runs faster but makes more mistakes than a handwritten proof
quiz.explain: The machine checks logic very reliably. But if the problem written for the machine drifts from the real one, the machine still says yes — only people can check the meaning.

well.label: The pebble well
well.art: An old stone well in the night garden, the moon shining straight down into it. Drag the moon and pebbles, each carved with the name of a problem, drop in one by one; ripples spread across the dark water, each pebble falling deeper than the last.
well.moonAria: Drag the moon, or use the ← → keys to move through the milestones

fact.text: OpenAI announced that an experimental model scored 35/42, gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO); three former IMO medallists graded it.
Gemini Deep Think scored 35/42, solving 5 of 6 problems; the IMO President confirmed it was a gold-medal score.
Levent Alpöge (Anthropic), with help from Claude Fable, gave a 3-dimensional counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, posed in 1939.
fact.verifiedBy: Archive of Formal Proofs (checked in Isabelle)

fact.text: OpenAI announced a proof that Navier–Stokes flow can “blow up”, with a version rewritten in Lean for machine checking.
OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts, grouped into 372 sets of results, from about 4,000 problems attempted; it warned that some still contain errors.
The Clay Institute only considers a prize once a solution is published in a qualifying outlet, at least two years have passed, and mathematicians broadly accept it.

horizon.text: The Math & AI advisory group at the IAS (Princeton): the future of mathematics cannot just be sitting and understanding results produced by AI labs.

insight.text: In just one year, AI went from Olympiad problems (07/2025) to a counterexample for a conjecture dating from 1939 (07/2026).

well.detail: Watch for the ◇ mark: many milestones are companies' own announcements. Where someone outside has checked, it says who.

vortex.label: Water that blows up
vortex.art: A pond as smooth as a mirror under the moon. The visitor stirs it once round: the water swirls, the eddies tighten towards one blinding point at the centre. Around the bank, tens of thousands of tiny fireflies swarm — each one an agent feeling its way.
vortex.stirAria: Stir the pond: drag in a circle, or hold an arrow key
vortex.leanNote: plus 17 hours rewriting it in Lean

insight.text: The Navier–Stokes equations describe how water and air flow. The million-dollar question: can a smooth flow suddenly “blow up”?

detail.text: OpenAI says about 10,000 agents ran for 88 hours on an unreleased model to find the proof; another AI took 17 more hours to rewrite it in Lean.

context.text: Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) and Levent Alpöge (Anthropic) posted a result on a closely related problem about 12 hours earlier; who came first is still disputed.
Both teams built on a strategy by mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, published in 2023.
The Clay Institute has not awarded the prize; OpenAI says it does not plan to accept the $1 million and has published the manuscript and Lean version for anyone to check.

mason.label: The mason who tests every stone
mason.art: Under a lantern, an old stonemason taps a small hammer on each step of a stone stair leading up the hill; a sound stone rings clear. At the top hangs a sign reading “the problem”, and beside it the original scroll to compare against.
mason.compare: Compare the sign with the original
mason.compareAria: Compare the problem written for the machine with the original problem
mason.original: Original: the sum of two odd numbers is even
mason.mismatch: The sign says “even numbers” — the machine checked correctly, but a different problem!

code.code:
-- Original: the sum of two odd numbers is even
theorem sum_even (a b : ℕ) (ha : Even a) (hb : Even b) :
    Even (a + b) := by
  exact Even.add ha hb

notes.text: A comment line: the problem a human wants to prove.
The problem as written for the machine. Notice: it says “Even”, not odd.
The machine checks this step: valid. But it has just proved a different problem.

codeNote.text: This code is a small Lean-style example AI Zen wrote for illustration, not taken from a real proof.

insights.text: Lean is a proof assistant: you write a proof the machine checks step by step; one wrong step and it refuses.
But people must still check the problem written in Lean is the real one: the machine checks logic, people check meaning.

detail.text: The Jacobian counterexample was checked again by an independent team in another proof assistant, Isabelle — two masons, two hammers.

circle.label: Four stones round the well
circle.art: Four stones stand round the moonlit well, each carved with a small line of text. Touch one and it glows, sending ripples to the middle of the well; when all four glow, the water stills and holds the whole moon.

stones.who: Charles Fefferman · Princeton, who wrote the official problem statement for the Clay Institute

view.text: “I'm very happy the problem is solved” — the man who wrote the problem welcomes the result, even though it still faces many rounds of checking.

stones.who: Tristan Buckmaster · NYU, the rival team

view.text: He called one of his own team's three papers “AI slop” and apologised: machine-written proofs can be very hard to read.

stones.who: Those asking about money and credit

view.text: According to Sébastien Bubeck (OpenAI), the proof hunt cost a few million dollars in compute; who came first, the two teams still don't agree.

stones.who: Math & AI advisory group · IAS, Princeton

view.text: This is “a significant event in mathematics” — but the future of mathematics cannot just be sitting and understanding results produced by AI labs.

common.text: Agreed: AI has done real mathematics, and it must be checked. Disputed: whose credit, at what cost, and what role people play.

insight.text: A maths result made by AI opens three questions: is it right, whose credit is it, and what is left for people to do.

quanta-ns.note: Independent reporting; the agent counts, run times and costs are OpenAI's own figures. The article says the result is still contested and people must still check the problem statement in Lean.

afp-jacobian.title: Formal Verification of an Explicit Counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture
afp-jacobian.publisher: Archive of Formal Proofs (Ramos, Hulak, de Queiroz)
afp-jacobian.note: Independent Isabelle/HOL check of the 3-dimensional map published by Levent Alpöge, crediting Claude Fable and Akhil Mathew (who posed the question). The 2-dimensional case remains open. The conjecture was posed by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939.
